title:
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome following appendicitis in a
young child: A case report and review of the pediatric literature
case_prompt:
An 11-year-old boy with no prior medical history was admitted with a 7-day history of fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting. On presentation his temperature was 36.8 °C, respiratory rate 32 /min, blood pressure 108/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He appeared drowsy and ill; abdominal examination revealed diffuse tenderness, distention, and rigidity. Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 30 400/mm3 with 32% bands. CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large perihepatic collection consistent with abscess, and he was diagnosed with complicated appendicitis. He underwent open laparotomy, appendectomy, and drain placement; intra-abdominal cultures grew Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus constellatus, and Bacteroides species. He improved and was weaned off vasopressors. His wound was closed by delayed primary closure.

On post-operative day 7, his blood pressures began rising; on day 9 the highest recorded blood pressure was 164/117 mm Hg (95th percentile for age/height/gender, 118/78 mm Hg). On day 10, he became drowsy and had two generalized tonic-clonic seizures treated with intravenous lorazepam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypodensities in the bilateral subcortical parietal regions. Brain MRI with FLAIR, MRA, and MRV revealed abnormal hyperintense signal predominantly in the bilateral parietal regions, extending into frontal and occipital lobes in the subcortical white matter, with associated gyral and leptomeningeal enhancement. There was no evidence of diffusion restriction, venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial hemorrhage, ring-enhancing lesions, or septic emboli.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious or autoimmune encephalitis was considered given the acute encephalopathy in a septic patient — “The differential diagnosis of PRES in children includes many conditions including infectious or autoimmune encephalitis…”  
2. Malignancy was considered as a cause of white-matter lesions — “…the differential diagnosis of PRES in children includes … malignancy…”  
3. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis was considered because of possible sepsis-related thrombosis but was excluded by MRV — “no venous sinus thrombosis…”  
4. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis was considered as a demyelinating encephalopathy — “…the differential diagnosis of PRES in children includes many conditions including … acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)…”  
5. Ischemic stroke was considered but was excluded by the absence of diffusion restriction on MRI — “There was no diffusion restriction…”  
6. Toxic leukoencephalopathy was considered in the differential given the imaging findings — “…the differential diagnosis of PRES in children includes many conditions including … toxic leukoencephalopathy.”
